items.q: When are corporate objectives agreed?
opts: After mission and after financial objectives
After mission and before financial objectives
Before mission and after financial objectives
Before mission and before financial objectives
items.why: The hierarchy: Mission (purpose/vision) comes first, then Corporate Objectives (whole-business targets), then Functional/Financial Objectives (departmental targets). So corporate objectives come after the mission but before financial objectives. The hierarchy flows: Mission -> Corporate Objectives -> Functional Objectives (including financial). Each level guides the next.
items.label: Past paper question

items.q: Which statement about profit is FALSE? A: Profit is a target for ALL businesses. B: Profit measures performance in triple bottom line. C: Profit rewards risk. D: Profit is a source of finance.
opts: Profit is a financial target for all businesses.
Profit is a measure of performance in Elkington's triple bottom line.
Profit is a reward for risk-taking.
Profit is a source of finance.
items.why: Not all businesses target profit. Social enterprises, charities, and not-for-profit organisations prioritise other objectives. The word 'all' makes this false.
items.label: Past paper question

items.q:
Statement 1: Retained profit appears on the statement of financial position as part of equity.
Statement 2: A bank overdraft is classified as a non-current liability on the statement of financial position.
opts: Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is false.
items.why: Retained profit (accumulated reserves) is part of shareholders' equity — Statement 1 is true. A bank overdraft is repayable on demand and is therefore a current liability, not a non-current liability — Statement 2 is false. Confusing overdrafts with long-term borrowing is a frequent student error.
items.label: New question

items.q: A company: 1) Identifies 'best in class', 2) Analyses its performance, 3) Uses analysis to improve. This is:
opts: Benchmarking
Centralisation
Kaizen
Protectionism
items.why: Benchmarking is the process of comparing your business against the best performers ('best in class') to identify gaps and improve. Benchmarking = comparing against the best. Kaizen = continuous small improvements.
items.label: Past paper question

items.q: Which of the following changes would most directly cause a business's inventory turnover (times) to increase?
opts: Negotiating longer payment terms with suppliers
Switching to a just-in-time stock management system
Increasing the selling price without changing the cost of sales
Extending credit terms offered to customers from 30 days to 60 days
items.why: Inventory turnover = cost of sales / average inventory. JIT reduces average inventory held, so for the same cost of sales, the ratio rises. Longer supplier payment terms affect payables days, not inventory turnover. Raising selling price changes revenue but not cost of sales or inventory directly. Extended customer credit affects receivables days.
items.label: New question

items.q: Transferring work to other businesses rather than completing it internally is known as:
opts: Fair trade
Lean production
Multi-channel distribution
Outsourcing
items.why: Outsourcing means contracting out business functions or processes to external third-party providers. Straightforward definition question. Outsourcing = getting someone else to do work you could do internally.
items.label: Past paper question

items.q: Vantage Sportswear Ltd wants to improve its operating profit margin without changing its revenue. Which of the following actions would most directly achieve this?
opts: Collecting payments from customers more quickly
Renegotiating supplier contracts to reduce the cost of raw materials
Increasing the credit period offered to trade customers
Repaying a long-term bank loan early
items.why: Reducing raw material costs lowers cost of sales, which raises gross profit and therefore operating profit for the same revenue, improving the operating margin. Faster collection and extended credit affect cash flow and working capital, not operating profit. Repaying a loan reduces interest charges, which affects profit before tax but not operating profit.
items.label: New question

items.q: Aurum Hotels plc has an operating profit margin of 20% but a profit-for-the-year margin of 11%. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the difference?
opts: The business has high variable costs relative to revenue, meaning that as occupancy levels fluctuate the cost of sales rises steeply, compressing margins at every level of the income statement.
The business has significant finance costs and a substantial corporation tax charge.
The business has written off a large amount of inventory during the year, which increases cost of sales and reduces both gross and operating profit margins by a broadly equal proportion.
The business's cost of sales has risen faster than revenue, squeezing the gross profit margin and causing each subsequent margin figure to be progressively lower than the operating profit margin.
items.why: The gap between operating profit margin and profit-for-the-year margin is explained by finance costs (interest) and taxation, both of which are deducted after operating profit in the income statement. Inventory write-offs and rising cost of sales would affect gross profit, and high variable costs affect gross margin, not the gap between operating and final profit.
items.label: New question

items.q: A manufacturer introduces robotic assembly lines, replacing a significant portion of its production workforce. Which of the following best describes the likely long-run effect on the firm's cost structure?
opts: Variable costs increase and fixed costs decrease, as the ongoing costs of robotic maintenance, software licensing, and periodic hardware upgrades fluctuate directly with output levels.
Both fixed and variable costs decrease immediately upon installation of the robots, as the capital outlay is offset by labour savings that take effect from the first day of operation.
Fixed costs increase and variable costs per unit decrease, as labour is replaced by capital.
Fixed costs decrease and the break-even output level falls, because eliminating the workforce removes the largest element of overhead expenditure from the firm's cost base.
items.why: Robots are capital equipment — a fixed cost. Replacing labour (a variable cost) with capital raises fixed costs but lowers variable costs per unit because fewer workers are needed per unit produced. This is a classic capital-for-labour substitution. Option A gets the relationship backwards. Option B ignores the capital investment required. Option D is incorrect because adding fixed costs raises the break-even point, not lowers it.
items.label: New question

items.q: Kendal Engineering Ltd has operating profit of £450,000. Its total equity is £1.8m and its non-current liabilities are £700,000. What is Kendal's return on capital employed (ROCE)?
items.why: Capital employed = total equity + non-current liabilities = £1.8m + £0.7m = £2.5m. ROCE = £450,000/£2,500,000 = 18%. A common error is to use only equity (giving 25%) or to use total assets rather than capital employed.
items.label: New question

items.q: Which of the following most accurately describes the role of a works council?
opts: A body that negotiates pay and conditions on behalf of workers through collective bargaining, using the threat of industrial action to secure improved terms from the employer.
A joint forum of employee and employer representatives that is consulted on business decisions such as redundancies and working practices.
A government agency responsible for investigating breaches of employment legislation, including failure to pay the national minimum wage and unlawful dismissal.
An elected committee of trade union representatives who coordinate strike action and work-to-rule campaigns when formal pay negotiations with management reach an impasse.
items.why: A works council is a consultative body where elected employee representatives and management meet to share information and discuss decisions affecting the workforce. It differs from a trade union in that it does not conduct collective bargaining over pay, and it is not a government body. Shop stewards and collective bargaining describe trade union activity.
items.label: New question

items.q: A product with a small share of a fast-growing market. According to the Boston Matrix, this is:
opts: A cash cow
A star
A dog
A question mark
items.why: Question Mark. Low market share + high growth = Question Mark. Needs significant investment to grow or risk becoming a Dog. Fast-growing = high growth. Small share = low share.
items.label: Past paper question

items.q:
Statement 1: A gearing ratio above 50% means that more than half of a business's capital employed is financed by long-term borrowing.
Statement 2: Issuing new ordinary shares to repay a long-term loan will reduce a company's gearing ratio.
opts: Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is false.
items.why: Gearing = non-current liabilities / capital employed × 100, so above 50% means debt exceeds equity in the capital structure — Statement 1 is true. Using the share issue proceeds to repay the loan reduces non-current liabilities and increases equity, both of which lower the gearing ratio — Statement 2 is true.
items.label: New question

items.q: A business collects information from a small group of customers about why they like a product. This is:
opts: Qualitative, primary market research
Qualitative, secondary market research
Quantitative, primary market research
Quantitative, secondary market research
items.why: Qualitative ('why they like' = opinions/reasons). Primary (business collects directly from customers). 'Why' = qualitative. Business collecting it itself = primary.
items.label: Past paper question

items.q: Hot drinks business adds cakes after focus group feedback. In Ansoff's matrix this is:
opts: Diversification from qualitative research
Diversification from quantitative research
Product development from qualitative research
Product development from quantitative research
items.why: Cakes are a new product for existing customers = product development. A focus group provides opinions/views = qualitative research (not numerical data). Focus group = qualitative (opinions, discussions). Survey with numbers = quantitative.
items.label: Past paper question

items.q: Statement 1: 'Market development = new product in new market.' Statement 2: 'Market penetration = existing product in existing market.'
opts: Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is false.
items.why: Statement 1 false: market development = existing product in new market (not new product). New product + new market = diversification. Statement 2 true: market penetration = existing product in existing market (increasing market share). Market development changes the market, not the product. New product + new market = diversification.
items.label: Past paper question

items.q: Statement 1: 'Penetration pricing is more likely if demand is price inelastic.' Statement 2: 'Price skimming is more likely if demand is price elastic.'
opts: Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is false.
items.why: Both false. Penetration = elastic (not inelastic). Skimming = inelastic (not elastic). Both statements have the elasticity backwards. Penetration = elastic. Skimming = inelastic.
items.label: Past paper question

items.q:
Statement 1: A business can increase its profit while its profitability falls.
Statement 2: Profitability is best measured by the absolute change in retained profit from one year to the next.
opts: Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is false. Statement 2 is false.
items.why: Profit can rise in absolute terms while revenue rises faster, so profit margin (a measure of profitability) falls — Statement 1 is true. Profitability is a relative measure, expressed as a margin or return, not as an absolute change in retained profit — Statement 2 is false. Students often confuse a rise in profit with improved profitability.
items.label: New question

items.q: Farida's Bakeries plc reports revenue of £2m, cost of sales of £800,000 and operating expenses (overheads) of £600,000. Which of the following correctly states the gross profit margin and operating profit margin?
opts: Gross profit margin 60%; operating profit margin 30%
Gross profit margin 40%; operating profit margin 30%
Gross profit margin 60%; operating profit margin 40%
Gross profit margin 40%; operating profit margin 60%
items.why: Gross profit = £2m − £0.8m = £1.2m; GPM = £1.2m/£2m = 60%. Operating profit = £1.2m − £0.6m = £0.6m; OPM = £0.6m/£2m = 30%. The most common error is to subtract overheads when calculating the gross margin or to divide by cost of sales rather than revenue.
items.label: New question

items.q: Factory: 120 units with 10 employees. Output increases 20%, costs increase 25%. Same employees. What happens to labour productivity and unit costs?
opts: Labour productivity rises and unit costs rise
Labour productivity rises and unit costs fall
Labour productivity falls and unit costs rise
Labour productivity falls and unit costs fall
items.why: LP = output/employees. Original: 120/10 = 12. New: 144/10 = 14.4. LP rises. Unit costs: output up 20% but costs up 25%. Costs rose faster than output, so unit costs rise. Output increased by 20% (good for LP) but total costs increased by 25% (bad for unit costs). Both productivity and costs can rise simultaneously.
items.label: Past paper question
